author: blu
body: This chapter used to carry its own copy of the fact log's shape: a header size of 78, a sector size of 512, its own sector-count formula, a writer that chained each field off the previous one's return value, and four readers that reached into a sector buffer at bare 32, 66 and 74. FactLog exists precisely so that shape has one definition, and DiskFacts was moved onto it -- but this chapter was left behind, which made FactLog's guarantee a half-truth. A change to the layout that DiskFacts followed and AppPersist did not is a divergence nothing would catch until a fact read back as garbage.

target: section:Sectors Are Relative To The Store
author: blu
body: Every sector number below is relative to the store's base LBA, exactly as in DiskFacts, and goes through that chapter's fact-read-at / fact-write-at. This chapter used to name absolute sectors, which on a partitioned disk is the partition table. A store carries the base it was opened against, so the base comes off the store rather than being resolved here.

author: blu
body: DiskFacts packs an entry whose kind is a FactKind; the kinds this chapter hands out are plain integers past that variant's range, so the packing is here rather than borrowed. What is NOT here is the layout: each field goes where FactLog says it goes.

author: blu
body: The old writer chained instead -- hash returns 32, the kind write returns 34, step over the gap with a bare + 32, and so on -- so the offsets were reachable only by adding the widths up in your head, and the 32-byte gap between the kind and the timestamp was a magic number in the middle of an expression. A writer that computes what a reader looks up is the same divergence with one side hidden. The gap is still there and still zero: the buffer is zeroed before anything is packed into it, and nothing writes those bytes.

author: blu
body: The two refusals are DiskFacts', for DiskFacts' reasons: a store whose base is negative sits on a disk that carries a partition table and no fact store, and a write that would run past the region's limit would land in whatever partition follows. Both answer the store UNCHANGED, so a caller watching disk-fact-count sees it fail to rise. This writer had neither guard and wrote straight through both.

target: section:Scan Two Kinds In Log Order
author: blu
body: Some readers need more than one kind, in the order the log wrote them -- a repository tree, for one, reads source definitions and their tombstones together, because which one is later for a given path is the whole question. This walks the log once and yields each matching entry tagged with its kind, in log order.

author: blu
body: The same walk, but from a given sector rather than the start of the log. An index snapshot covers the log up to a sector; rebuilding on top of it needs only the entries written after that point, so a fast rebuild scans the tail instead of the whole log. The start sector is a fact boundary (it was the log-head captured when the snapshot was taken), so the walk lands cleanly on the first entry that the snapshot did not already fold in.

author: blu
body: Compaction used to keep ONE FACT PER KIND. It walked the log and dropped any entry whose kind it had already seen, so a store with five hundred facts of the same kind compacted down to one and the other four hundred and ninety-nine were gone.

author: blu
body: That is the right answer for a kind that holds a single current value -- the browser's history blob is rewritten whole each time, and only the newest is worth keeping -- and it is a catastrophe for a kind that holds a collection. Kind 24 is secret ENTRIES. Kind 25 is FileShare manifests. Kind 26 is revocation records. Kind 30 is every source definition in the repository. All of them are collections, and compacting any of them would have destroyed all but one member.

author: blu
body: The log cannot tell the difference. Nothing on the disk says that fact B supersedes fact A; a fact is a kind, a timestamp, a hash and some bytes. Guessing the relation from the kind is how you lose a repository, and the kind space already contains counterexamples.

author: blu
body: So the rule is the conservative one, and it is the only one the data supports: a compactor that cannot prove two facts are the same must keep them both. Identity for a content-addressed fact is its content hash, which is already in the entry header -- so two entries collapse only when they are the same kind AND the same hash, which is to say the same bytes written twice. Nothing else is ever dropped.

author: blu
body: The consequence is honest and worth stating: compaction no longer reclaims space from a superseded singleton, because the disk holds no evidence that it was superseded, and the conservative rule is the correct trade. Reclaiming space is what the archive base is for -- a signed, compressed copy of a range of the log, recorded in the live log as the base (Works chapter FactArchive) -- and it does not guess at supersession either: it moves history to another tier rather than deciding that any of it is redundant.

author: blu
body: The old walk had a second defect. It collected survivors newest-first and handed them straight to compact-rewrite, so a compacted log came out REVERSED -- and app-scan-last, which trusts log order to mean recency, would then have returned the OLDEST fact of a kind. Survivors are restored to log order here.
